newsitem.title: JORDAN: British jet car in "gentle" 260 mph desert trial.
newsitem.headline: British jet car in "gentle" 260 mph desert trial.

text.p: Britain's jet-powered car Thrust SSC roared across the deserts of southern Jordan on Tuesday on its first trial for an attempt to break the world land speed record.

In fading afternoon light British Royal Air Force pilot Andy Green drove the 9.5-tonne car, powered by twin jets from a Phantom warplane, up to a modest 260 miles per hour (416 kph), a fraction of the speed the car is aiming to reach.
"This was basically just a gentle first run," project leader and current world record holder Richard Noble said after Green's half-minute outing on the parched mudflats of al-Jafr.
"We were shooting for 300 (mph), but the light itself wasn't too good," he told Reuters.

Noble hopes the Thrust jet-car will break his own record of 633.47 mph (1,019.44 kph) in Jordan before he takes it to Nevada in the United States next year for a run at the sound barrier -- about 750 mph (1,200 kph).
Noble said it was too early to say when the team would challenge for the record, adding that they would spend the next day checking information provided by Tuesday's half-minute run.
He said they could now work out the resistance from the desert floor on the car's aluminium wheels, and assess how quickly the car would slow from top speeds on the 10 mile (16 km) track.
"This is a crucial run. It's given us a load of data on the car," Noble said. "Now we can calculate just how fast we can safely go...without wrecking the car in the rocks at the end of the track."
Earlier on Tuesday the car was taken from the military airbase where the team have spent the last two weeks finetuning its 110,000 horsepower engines.
"We had a hell of a struggle to get the car out here," Noble said.

The 16-metre (50-foot) long machine was driven past camels and about 100 curious villagers before arriving at the test site, where 17 lines, each 10 miles long, have been drawn on the desert floor for the car to follow.
To reach the speed of sound and still have time for its parachute brakes to slow it, the car would need a track of over 15 miles (22.5 km).
